newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Bolger hints at compromise in quest for govt.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Bolger hints at compromise in quest for govt.

text.p: Prime Minister Jim Bolger hinted on Sunday he is prepared to make changes to find a coalition partner in his quest to form a new government.

"I have no doubt that New Zealand in general supports the policies that have been followed for the last few years," he told Radio New Zealand's Morning Report just hours after vote counting ended in Saturday's general election.
"Clearly there are a number of issues that New Zealanders also want to have addressed in a slightly different way than they have been in the last little while."

While the election gave National the most seats with 44, it gave the three main opposition parties 67 seats in the 120-seat parliament. It left New Zealand First, which has not committed to Labour on the left or National on the right, with 17 seats and the role of kingmaker.
Bolger will lead a caretaker government until a new government is formed, possibly not until December.
"I'm not making any predictions. It's now time for calm heads and sensible judgements and I will do my damnedest to exercise those," Bolger said.
He said he would need to form a coalition unless he was able to form a minority government.
"I will initiate discussions with a variety of people and then we will determine what is the way forward.
"I expect to speak to a number of people today and New Zealand First could be one of those," he said.
"If it is not today it will be in the next 24 hours."
Bolger said there was clearly a huge amount of negotiation required. On some policy issues there were significant differences.
Any coalition would have to be formed on the basis of consultation, compromise and commonsense, he said.
"I see those as the three ingredients that have to be brought to the table if we are to find a solution and produce a sound government for New Zealand."
Asked if he could see a way through to agreement with New Zealand First, Bolger said NZ First had by far the most rational economic policy of the three parties of the left.
"They were closer to the centre party in terms of a position somewhere between the National Party and Labour Party. Their spending promises were much less and in a number of other areas."
Bolger said he was confident he could exclude personality conflicts from any discussions with NZ First leader Winston Peters. He sacked Peters from his cabinet in 1992.
Asked about his own position as leader of National, he said:
"I think there is still a lot to be offered to politics in New Zealand and I'd like to be around for a little while yet, quite a long while yet."
